title: The travel pack
description: Stick packs sized exactly for a water bottle. You've grabbed these at an airport kiosk without thinking about it.

title: Strain scores as mood rings
description: Someone you follow posts their recovery graph every morning like a weather report for their body.

title: The cooler wall
description: A full row of slim cans at the gym cooler, each flavor louder than the last. The branding is doing reps.

title: One scoop, whole morning
description: The green scoop, the shaker, the promise that this one glass replaces six other pills.

title: 69% Sugar by Weight
description: Critic math against WHO's oral-rehydration ratio finds the flagship overshoots the glucose it prescribes — sweetness is a palate decision, not a hydration requirement. Health halos rarely survive a label audit.

title: The Nightlife Nod
description: Four marketed occasions — heat, exercise, travel, nightlife — circle the hangover use consumers actually meme about, without ever saying the word. Positioning can sell a use case by winking at it instead of claiming it.

title: The Watney Save — 2 A.M.
description: One pro golfer's overnight respiratory-rate spike flagged an infection before symptoms, and the tour handed out a thousand straps. A single true save story can carry years of guardian-brand reassurance.

title: Rent Your Biometrics: $1.1B Run-Rate
description: Tier prices sit beside doubled bookings: hardware comes "free" because you subscribe to your own vital signs, and new features gate old ones. The ledger shows who really owns the device on your wrist.

title: "Burns Body Fat" — Mind the Asterisk
description: Accelerate metabolism, burn fat: FDA-permitted structure/function language that sounds medical yet needs no drug approval — exactly the gap plaintiffs say misleads. Wellness copy often borrows medicine's tone, not its proof.

title: The Paid Campus Tribe
description: CELSIUS University ambassadors and NIL college athletes make the fitness tribe feel found rather than bought — until you notice the roster is salaried. Community marketing lands hardest while the W-2s stay quiet.

title: The Fourteenth Ad Read
description: Verbatim host-read spots with personal promo codes expose the machine: hundreds of podcasts, 20–50% affiliate cuts, per-host landing pages. Attribution — not the scoop — was the product being perfected.

title: $79 a Month, Renewing Nicely
description: A monthly invoice flanked by a welcome gift kit and a 90-day guarantee lays out the DTC playbook: gifts de-risk trial, discounts steer you into recurring billing. The receipt is where the relationship's terms turn honest.

title: Your gift card is their working capital
description: Quarterly gift-card loads run $2.6–3.6B and stored cards touch roughly 43–47% of transactions — about $11–13B a year prepaid before any latte is poured. Loyalty isn't only a program; the float is a financing engine sweetened by breakage.

title: The wrong-name curve
description: Studies dubbed "the Starbucks effect" found name-based orders beat order numbers by reducing objectification — until a wrong name crashed satisfaction below anonymous service. Personalization pays only while it feels like respect.

title: Rest has a dress code
description: A $950 Gucci edition sold out while base-ring waitlists stretched — proof the ring sells aspiration first, metrics second. Health tracking reframed as jewelry prices the tribe out of its own movement.

title: Three days before symptoms
description: "Over 90% accuracy up to three days before symptoms" was a research platform's result, never an FDA-authorized disease-detection claim — yet the NBA ordered 2,000+ rings for its bubble. Perception can outrun regulation.

title: The churn trio
description: Aggregated user reports flag rates "not made clear," hard cancellation, and upsell fatigue running beneath the Apple-award halo. Retention friction quietly taxes a brand that promises effortlessness.

title: Binaural beats on trial
description: A systematic review found 8 of 14 studies contradicting binaural-beat entrainment, and an audit flagged 92.5% of streaming sound-therapy tracks for deviant claims. When the feature story outruns the evidence, the brand inherits the doubt.

title: Content Is the Ad Budget
description: Red Bull stopped renting airtime and built its own: a media house, a magazine read by millions, hundreds of stories a year — marketing spend that ends up as sellable programming instead of vanished commercials. The most advanced ad budget is one that becomes an asset.

title: $13M for Wings
description: In 2014 Red Bull paid a $13M settlement over "gives you wings," withdrawing the challenged claims while keeping the slogan that made them famous. Puffery rides a legal line — and even when the law trims the claim, the myth usually survives the fine.

title: +22% Deep Sleep*
description: "Users gained 22% more deep sleep" is a real published number — from one week, fifty-four people, in a study run by the company selling the bed, measuring effects its own authors call transient. A true statistic can still be marketing; read what the asterisk is holding up.

title: Year Five: $6,900
description: A $2,599 mattress cover quietly compounds to roughly $6,900 after five years of mandatory membership — and lapse on payment, and the smart bed stops being smart. The sticker price sells the dream; the subscription is where the bill actually lives.

title: 3M Views Before the First Can
description: Before Liquid Death sold a single can, a fake Facebook page and a $1,500 ad pulled three million views and eighty thousand followers. The audience came first and the product was built for people already gathered — demand can be manufactured before inventory.

title: Can Autopsy: Plastic Inside
description: Slice open an anti-plastic icon and every can hides a plastic liner — now the subject of a class action alleging "Death to Plastic" misleads. When a brand builds identity on an enemy it cannot live without, expect the materials to get audited.

title: Cut the Ads, Kept the Boom
description: Mid-viral-summer 2019 White Claw cut ad spend roughly 30% while July sales nearly quadrupled — the internet was selling the brand better than the brand was. Earned media can out-punch paid, but fame you didn't make isn't fame you control.

title: Alcohol Is Still Alcohol
description: The can's math checks out — about 100 calories, ~2g carbs — yet clinicians note 5% ABV "goes down like water," topping many beers. Accurate labels wrapped in an implication: light equals healthy does the heavy lifting.

title: "Non-Alcoholic" Means Up to 0.5%
description: Legally, non-alcoholic beer is a range, not chemical zero — and independent testing has caught NoLo drinks running over their labels. For most drinkers it's trivia; for someone in recovery, the fine print is the whole story.

title: $9.99 vs $13.99
description: Six-packs priced three or four dollars above rival NA beers — the premium funds two purpose-built breweries nobody else bothered to build. A mission can justify margin, but on the shelf it quietly gates the "for all times" crowd.

title: Even When They Ask Us
description: The pledge is real — no paid influencers, ever — and nearly irrelevant: an unpaid creator army minted "upper decky lip pillows" and a richer mythology than any agency could buy. The most valuable media plan may be the one you don't control.

title: Authorized ≠ Approved
description: A first in history: the FDA cleared 20 ZYN pouches as lower-risk for adults who smoke. But authorized isn't approved — nothing in the aisle is cleared to treat nicotine dependence. Regulator grammar becomes a health halo in passing.

title: Who Owns "Independent"?
description: Seedlip's farm myth outlived its farmer — majority-Diageo since 2019 — and by 2024 challenger Ritual joined the same owner: both sides of the zero-proof shelf, one boardroom. Authenticity kept selling long after independence stopped being true.

title: The Mixer Subsidy
description: Nearly every serve adds bubbles — tonic, soda, citrus — so part of what you taste arrives from someone else's bottle while value migrates down the shelf. Spirit-tier pricing has to argue itself forever against a five-dollar mixer doing the heavy lifting.
